title: Meine Stadt (My Town)
description: Talk about places in town, ask for and give directions, describe your way to school, and use transport phrases with mit and zu.

notes.heading: Places in Town — Orte in der Stadt
notes.body:
Here are the most important words for places in a town. Learn each word together with its article (der / die / das).

| German | English |
|---|---|
| der Bahnhof | the train station |
| das Kino | the cinema |
| die Schule | the school |
| der Marktplatz | the market square |
| die Post | the post office |
| das Schwimmbad | the swimming pool |
| die Kirche | the church |
| das Rathaus | the town hall |
| der Supermarkt | the supermarket |
| die Bibliothek | the library |

💡 Example: *Das Kino ist groß.* — The cinema is big.

⚠️ Common mistake: forgetting the capital letter. All German nouns are capitalised: *das Kino*, never *das kino*.

notes.heading: Asking the Way — Wo ist ...?
notes.body:
To ask where something is, use **Wo ist ...?** for one place.

- *Wo ist der Bahnhof?* — Where is the station?
- *Wo ist das Schwimmbad?* — Where is the swimming pool?
- *Wo sind die Toiletten?* — Where are the toilets? (plural → **sind**)

Handy answers for now:

| German | English |
|---|---|
| hier | here |
| dort / da drüben | there / over there |
| in der Nähe | nearby |
| weit weg | far away |

💡 Worked example:
- *Entschuldigung, wo ist die Post?* — Excuse me, where is the post office?
- *Die Post ist hier in der Nähe.* — The post office is near here.

✅ Check: *Wo ist ...?* uses **ist** with one thing; *Wo sind ...?* uses **sind** with more than one.

notes.heading: Giving Directions — links, rechts, geradeaus
notes.body:
The three core direction words:

| German | English |
|---|---|
| links | left |
| rechts | right |
| geradeaus | straight ahead |

Build fuller directions with these patterns:

- *Gehen Sie geradeaus.* — Go straight ahead. (polite)
- *Geh links.* — Go left. (informal, to a friend)
- *Die erste Straße rechts.* — The first street on the right.
- *Die zweite Straße links.* — The second street on the left.
- *an der Ecke* — at the corner

💡 Worked example: *Gehen Sie geradeaus, dann die erste Straße links. Der Bahnhof ist an der Ecke.* — Go straight ahead, then the first street on the left. The station is at the corner.

📎 Key point: use ordinal numbers (*die erste, die zweite, die dritte Straße*) to say which street to take.

notes.heading: Getting Around — Transport with mit and zu Fuß
notes.body:
To say how you travel, German uses **mit** + article:

| German | English |
|---|---|
| mit dem Bus | by bus |
| mit der Bahn / mit dem Zug | by train |
| mit dem Auto | by car |
| mit dem Fahrrad | by bike |
| mit der U-Bahn | by underground |
| zu Fuß | on foot (no *mit*!) |

💡 Worked example: *Ich fahre mit dem Bus zur Schule.* — I go to school by bus.

⚠️ Common mistake: saying *mit dem Fuß*. On foot is always the fixed phrase **zu Fuß**.

✅ Check: after **mit**, masculine and neuter words use **dem** (*mit dem Bus*, *mit dem Auto*); feminine words use **der** (*mit der Bahn*).

notes.heading: My Way to School — Mein Schulweg
notes.body:
To describe your route, chain short sentences with time-order words:

| German | English |
|---|---|
| zuerst | first |
| dann | then |
| danach | after that |
| schließlich / am Ende | finally / at the end |

💡 Worked example: *Zuerst gehe ich zu Fuß zur Haltestelle. Dann fahre ich mit dem Bus in die Stadt. Danach gehe ich links und schließlich bin ich an der Schule.* — First I walk to the bus stop. Then I take the bus into town. After that I turn left and finally I am at school.

📎 Key point: **zuerst, dann, danach** come first in the sentence, so the verb comes second and the subject follows the verb: *Dann fahre ich ...* — the word order is time word + verb + subject.

notes.heading: Separable Verbs — an Introduction
notes.body:
Some German verbs have a prefix that splits off and jumps to the end of the sentence. You already know two patterns like this:

- **losfahren** = to set off / depart → *Der Bus fährt um acht Uhr los.* — The bus departs at eight o'clock.
- **abholen** = to pick up / fetch → *Ich hole meinen Bruder ab.* — I pick up my brother.
- **einkaufen** = to shop → *Wir kaufen am Samstag ein.* — We shop on Saturday.

🔑 How it works: the main part of the verb goes in the normal verb position (second place); the prefix goes to the very end of the sentence.

💡 *Ich fahre um sieben Uhr los und hole dann meine Freundin ab.* — I set off at seven and then pick up my friend.

⚠️ Common mistake: keeping the prefix attached — *Ich losfahre um acht* is wrong. The prefix must separate: *Ich fahre ... los.*

notes.heading: Prepositions: mit, zu, in
notes.body:
Three little words do a lot of work in this topic:

- **mit** = with / by (transport): *mit dem Bus, mit der Bahn, mit meinem Vater*
- **zu** = to (a place or person): *zur Schule* (zu + der = zur), *zum Bahnhof* (zu + dem = zum)
- **in** = to / into (a place you enter): *in die Schule, in das Kino (ins Kino), in die Stadt*

💡 Worked examples:
- *Ich fahre mit dem Zug zum Bahnhof.* — I take the train to the station.
- *Wir gehen ins Kino.* — We are going to the cinema.

📎 Key points to remember:
- **zu + dem = zum**, **zu + der = zur**, **in + das = ins** — German loves these short forms.
- Use **zu** for destinations in general and **in** when you go inside a building or a place.

flashcards.example: Wo ist der Bahnhof? — Where is the station?
Das Kino ist in der Stadt. — The cinema is in town.
Der Marktplatz ist sehr alt. — The market square is very old.
Die Post ist hier in der Nähe. — The post office is nearby.
Am Samstag gehe ich ins Schwimmbad. — On Saturday I go to the swimming pool.
Die Schule ist rechts. — The school is on the right.
Geh geradeaus bis zur Kirche. — Go straight ahead as far as the church.
Ich fahre mit dem Bus zur Schule. — I go to school by bus.
Kommst du zu Fuß? — Are you coming on foot?

flashcards.definition: Where is ...? — the question to ask for a place
flashcards.example: Entschuldigung, wo ist die Post? — Excuse me, where is the post office?

flashcards.definition: to set off, to depart — a separable verb
flashcards.example: Der Zug fährt um neun Uhr los. — The train departs at nine o'clock.

questions.explanation: Der Bahnhof is the train station — the place where trains (Züge) arrive and depart.
Geradeaus means straight ahead. Links is left and rechts is right.

questions.stem: How do you ask "Where is the post office?" in German?
questions.explanation: Wo ist ...? asks where something is, and die Post is the post office. Wie means how, was means what, and sind is only for plurals.
On foot is the fixed phrase zu Fuß. Unlike transport with mit (mit dem Bus), German never says mit dem Fuß.

questions.stem: Choose the correct translation: "I go to school by bus."
choices: Ich fahre mit dem Bus zur Schule.
Ich gehe mit dem Bus zur Schule.
Ich fahre mit die Bus zur Schule.
Ich fahre zu Bus in die Schule.
questions.explanation: By bus is mit dem Bus (der Bus → dem after mit), and fahren is the verb for travelling by vehicle. Option 2 uses gehen (on foot), and options 3 and 4 break the article rules.

questions.stem: Which sentence has the correct word order?
choices: Dann ich fahre mit dem Zug.
Dann fahre ich mit dem Zug.
Dann mit dem Zug ich fahre.
Dann ich mit dem Zug fahre.
questions.explanation: When a time word like dann starts the sentence, the verb stays in second position and the subject follows it: Dann fahre ich ...

questions.stem: "Ich hole meinen Bruder ab." — What does this sentence mean?
questions.explanation: Abholen means to pick up / fetch. It is a separable verb, so ab moves to the end of the sentence: Ich hole ... ab.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: "_____ gehe ich zu Fuß, _____ fahre ich mit dem Bus."
questions.explanation: Zuerst (first) ... dann (then) is the natural sequence for describing a route in steps.

questions.stem: "Die zweite Straße links" tells you to:
choices: take the second street on the left
take the second street on the right
take the first street on the left
questions.explanation: Zweite is the ordinal number second, and links is left — so you take the second street on the left.

questions.stem: Which is the correct separable-verb sentence?
choices: Der Bus losfährt um acht Uhr.
Der Bus fährt los um acht Uhr an.
Der Bus fährt um acht Uhr los.
Der Bus um acht Uhr fährt los.
questions.explanation: Losfahren is separable: the conjugated part (fährt) takes the second position and the prefix los goes to the very end — Der Bus fährt um acht Uhr los.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich fahre mit _____ U-Bahn ins Zentrum."
questions.explanation: Die U-Bahn is feminine, and after mit a feminine noun takes der: mit der U-Bahn. Dem is for masculine and neuter nouns after mit.

questions.stem: A friend gives you these directions: "Geh geradeaus, dann die erste Straße rechts. Das Kino ist an der Ecke." What must you do?
choices: Go straight, turn right at the first street; the cinema is on the corner
Turn right immediately; the cinema is straight ahead
Go straight, turn left at the first street; the cinema is nearby
Go straight past two corners; the cinema is on the right
questions.explanation: Geradeaus = straight ahead; die erste Straße rechts = the first street on the right; an der Ecke = on the corner.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly combines a transport phrase with a destination?
choices: Wir fahren mit dem Auto zum Bahnhof.
Wir fahren mit das Auto zum Bahnhof.
Wir gehen mit dem Auto zur Bahnhof.
Wir fahren zu Auto zum Bahnhof.
questions.explanation: Das Auto becomes dem after mit (mit dem Auto), and der Bahnhof becomes dem after zu (zum Bahnhof). Fahren is correct because you travel by car.

questions.stem: Which question is correct if you are looking for the toilets (plural)?
questions.explanation: Die Toiletten is plural, so the verb must be sind: Wo sind die Toiletten? Ist is for singular nouns; bist and seid only go with du and ihr.

questions.stem: "Entschuldigung, wo ist der Marktplatz?" is best translated as:
choices: Sorry, where was the market square?
Excuse me, where is the market square?
Excuse me, how is the market square?
Please, where are the market squares?
questions.explanation: Entschuldigung is the polite way to get someone's attention (excuse me), and Wo ist der Marktplatz? asks where the market square is.
